entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Julius Iullus was a member of the ancient patrician gens Julia, one of the most influential and powerful families in the Roman Republic. His family's wealth and status allowed him to pursue a career in politics, and he quickly rose through the ranks, becoming consul in 430 BC at the age of 44. This achievement was significant not only for Iullus but also for his family, as it solidified their position as one of the most prominent patrician families in Rome.


Iullus's military career was marked by his service as magister equitum in 431 BC, a position that gave him command of the Roman cavalry. This experience likely helped him develop the skills and strategic thinking that would serve him well in his later years. In 438 BC, Iullus was appointed as one of the consular tribunes, a position that gave him a say in the governance of Rome. This role would have allowed him to exert significant influence over the city's politics, particularly in the areas of law and justice.


Despite his many achievements, Iullus's life remains somewhat of a mystery. His birth and death dates are unknown, and few details are known about his personal life. However, his legacy as a member of the gens Julia and his contributions to Roman politics and military affairs are well-documented. He is remembered as a notable figure in the history of ancient Rome, a testament to the enduring power and influence of the patrician class.


The inscription on his tomb, 'Lucius Julius Iullus, son of Lucius Julius, from the gens Julia', serves as a poignant reminder of the importance of family and heritage in ancient Roman culture. His story is a fascinating glimpse into the lives of the patrician class, a group of individuals who played a pivotal role in shaping the course of Roman history.
